items.visual: Death Valley is a desert in California. It gets only about two inches of rain in a year. In summer, the temperature there can rise above 120 degrees Fahrenheit. Some tough plants and animals still live there.

choices.t: It gets only about two inches of rain in a year.
choices.why: This shows the desert is dry, not how hot it is.

choices.t: In summer, the temperature there can rise above 120 degrees Fahrenheit.
Some tough plants and animals still live there.
choices.why: This is about living things, not temperature.

items.explain: The claim is about heat. "Above 120 degrees" is the only sentence about temperature. 🌡️
items.hint: Which sentence gives a temperature?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that dolphins are smart?
items.visual: Dolphins are mammals that live in the ocean. They breathe air through a blowhole on top of their heads. Scientists have seen dolphins use sea sponges to protect their noses while they search for food. Dolphins often swim in groups called pods.

choices.t: They breathe air through a blowhole on top of their heads.
choices.why: This is about breathing, not about being smart.

choices.t: Dolphins often swim in groups called pods.
choices.why: This is about how they travel, not about being smart.

choices.t: Scientists have seen dolphins use sea sponges to protect their noses while they search for food.

items.explain: Using an object as a tool takes smart thinking. That proves the claim. 🐬
items.hint: Which sentence shows a dolphin solving a problem?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that Ethan is responsible?
items.visual: Ethan's class got a pet hamster named Nutmeg. Ethan asked to be her helper. Every morning, he gave Nutmeg fresh food and water without being reminded. Ethan thinks hamsters are cute.

choices.t: Every morning, he gave Nutmeg fresh food and water without being reminded.
Ethan's class got a pet hamster named Nutmeg.
choices.why: This tells about the class pet, not about Ethan.
Thinking a pet is cute does not show he takes care of it.

items.explain: Being responsible means doing your job without being told. Ethan fed Nutmeg every morning without being reminded. 🐹
items.hint: Responsible means doing your job every time.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that recycling cans saves energy?
items.visual: Aluminum cans can be recycled again and again. Making a new can from a recycled can uses much less energy than making one from new metal. A recycled can may be back on a store shelf in about two months. Many cities pick up recycling each week.

choices.t: A recycled can may be back on a store shelf in about two months.
choices.why: This is about how fast it happens, not about energy.

choices.t: Making a new can from a recycled can uses much less energy than making one from new metal.
Many cities pick up recycling each week.
choices.why: This is about pickup, not about energy.

items.explain: The claim is about energy. Only this sentence says recycling uses much less energy. ♻️
items.hint: Which sentence uses the word energy?

items.prompt: Which sentence shows that young sunflowers follow the Sun?
items.visual: Sunflowers can grow taller than a grown-up. Young sunflower plants turn their heads to face the Sun as it moves across the sky. Their seeds are a favorite food for birds. Sunflowers grow best in warm, sunny places.

choices.t: Sunflowers grow best in warm, sunny places.
choices.why: This is true, but it shows sunflowers like sun, not that they move to follow it.

choices.t: Young sunflower plants turn their heads to face the Sun as it moves across the sky.
Their seeds are a favorite food for birds.
choices.why: This is about seeds, not about following the Sun.

items.explain: Following the Sun means turning as the Sun moves. Only this sentence says that. 🌻
items.hint: Which sentence tells about the plant moving?

situations.s: Leo's block tower fell down. His face is red. His hands are in fists.
o: Frustrated or angry
Yes! A red face and fists are clues for a strong, upset feeling.
Happy
Happy people usually smile and look relaxed. Look at the clues again: red face, fists.
Sleepy
Sleepy people yawn and rub their eyes. Leo has fists and a red face.

situations.s: Ana is smiling. She is jumping up and down. It is her birthday.
o: Excited
Yes! Smiling and jumping are clues for excited. Birthdays are exciting!
Scared
Scared people often freeze or hide. Ana is smiling and jumping.
Bored
Bored people sigh and look away. Ana is jumping with a big smile.

situations.s: Sam is sitting alone. He is looking down. His lip is shaking.
o: Sad
Yes! Looking down, sitting alone and a shaking lip are clues for sad.
Silly
Silly people laugh and make funny faces. These clues show a different feeling.
Proud
Proud people stand tall and smile. Sam is looking down.

situations.s: Priya is hiding behind her mom. It is her first day at a new school.
o: Nervous or shy
Yes! New places can feel scary. Hiding is a clue for nervous or shy.
Angry
Angry people may yell or make fists. Priya is hiding quietly.
Excited
Excited people often run toward things. Priya is hiding.

situations.s: A big dog barked right next to Max. Max's eyes are wide. He jumped back.
o: Scared
Yes! Wide eyes and jumping back are clues for scared.
Happy
A loud surprise usually does not feel happy. Look at his eyes and body.
Tired
Tired people move slowly. Max jumped back fast.

situations.s: You are telling your friend a long story. She yawns and looks around the room.
o: Tired, or ready for a new topic
Yes! Yawning and looking away are clues. You could ask: "Do you want to talk about something else?"
Very excited about your story
Excited listeners usually look at you and ask questions. Yawning is a different clue.
Angry at you
Angry people may frown or cross their arms. Yawning usually means tired or bored, not angry.

situations.s: You tell Grandpa a joke. He laughs and gives you a high five.
o: Happy. He liked the joke!
Yes! Laughing and a high five are clues that he enjoyed it.
Upset
Upset people do not usually laugh and high five. Those are happy clues.
Scared
Scared people do not usually laugh and high five.

situations.s: The tip of your pencil breaks.
situations.why: Small problem. You can fix it yourself: sharpen it or get a new pencil.

situations.s: Someone took the red crayon you wanted.
situations.why: Small problem. You can use another color, or wait and ask for a turn.

situations.s: You lost a game at recess.
situations.why: Small problem. Losing feels bad for a moment, but you can play again tomorrow.

situations.s: You feel sick at school and your tummy hurts a lot.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell your teacher so a grown-up can help you.

situations.s: You left your homework at home.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell your teacher. Together you can make a plan.

situations.s: A classmate fell off the slide and is hurt.
situations.why: Big problem. Get a grown-up right away.

situations.s: The fire alarm is ringing.
situations.why: Big problem. Stay calm and follow your teacher right away.

situations.s: You spilled a little water on your desk.
situations.why: Small problem. Get a paper towel and wipe it up.

situations.s: Your pencil broke during a test.
situations.q: Which reaction matches the size of the problem?
o: Say "oh well" and sharpen it
Yes! A small problem gets a small reaction.
Scream and throw the pencil
That is a big reaction for a small problem. It could scare others or get you in trouble.
Cry for the rest of the day
That is a big reaction for a small problem. A new pencil fixes it.

situations.s: Your juice box spilled a little at lunch.
situations.q: Which reaction matches the size of the problem?
o: Get a napkin and wipe it up
Yes! Small problem, small reaction. Problem solved!
Yell "This is the worst day ever!"
That is a big reaction for a small problem. A napkin can fix it.
Hide under the table
That is a big reaction. A napkin can fix it quickly.

situations.s: The classroom is very loud and your ears hurt.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Cover your ears or ask for a quiet break
Yes! Taking care of your ears is smart. Asking for a break is a great tool.
Yell "BE QUIET!"
Yelling makes it even louder, and others may feel upset.
Run out of the room without telling anyone
Grown-ups need to know where you are to keep you safe. Ask for a break instead.

situations.s: You lost a game and you feel very angry.
situations.q: What is a good way to calm down?
o: Take 5 slow breaths
Yes! Slow breaths tell your body it is safe. Then the angry feeling gets smaller.
Hit the table
Hitting can hurt you or break things. The angry feeling does not go away.
Shout "You cheated!"
Blaming others can hurt their feelings. Calm your body first.

situations.s: Your body feels wiggly and you cannot sit still in class.
o: Ask for a movement break or squeeze a fidget
Yes! Some bodies need to move. Asking for a break is a smart tool.
Poke the person next to you
Poking can bother or hurt others. Use a fidget or ask for a break.
Roll on the floor during the lesson
That can stop the class. Ask for a movement break instead.

situations.s: You feel worried about a test tomorrow.
o: Tell a grown-up and make a plan together
Yes! Talking about worries makes them smaller. A plan helps your brain feel ready.
Hide the test paper
Hiding does not make the worry go away. A grown-up can help.
Keep the worry a secret
Worries often grow when we keep them inside. Sharing helps.

situations.s: The field trip is cancelled because of rain. You were really excited.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Feel disappointed, take a breath, and ask about the new plan
Yes! It is OK to feel disappointed. Then find out Plan B.
Refuse to do anything all day
That makes the whole day hard. Plan B can still be fun.
Scream until they change it back
Screaming cannot stop the rain. Calm down, then ask about Plan B.

situations.s: On your feelings thermometer, you are at 5 out of 5. You are very, very upset.
o: Calm your body first, then solve the problem
Yes! When feelings are at 5, the thinking brain needs a break first. Breathe, then solve.
Solve the problem right now while yelling
It is very hard to think when you are that upset. Calm first, then solve.
Tell everyone they are wrong
That can make the problem bigger. Calm your body first.

situations.s: Your friend says: "I went to the beach this weekend!"
o: "Cool! What did you see there?"
Yes! You asked about HER topic. That keeps the ping-pong going.
"Volcanoes can be 1,000 degrees! Lava is..."
Volcanoes are cool, but this changes the topic. First ask about her beach trip.
Say nothing and walk away
She might feel ignored. Try asking a question back.

situations.s: You are telling a friend about octopuses. She looks away and says "uh-huh" in a flat voice.
o: She might want a turn or a new topic
Yes! Looking away and a flat voice are clues. You can ask what she wants to talk about.
She wants 10 more octopus facts
Looking away can mean she wants a change, but not always. The best way to know is to ask her!
She is angry at octopuses
It is probably not about octopuses. She might just want a turn to talk.

situations.s: You love sharks. You have told your friend 5 shark facts already.
situations.q: What is a good thing to say next?
o: "Do you want to hear more, or talk about something else?"
Yes! Checking is kind. Your friend gets to choose, too.
Keep talking louder
Talking louder does not help your friend enjoy it more. Check in with a question.
Stop talking forever
You do not need to stop forever! Just check if your friend wants more.

situations.s: Two kids are talking about their dogs. You want to join.
situations.q: What is a good way to join?
o: Wait for a pause, then say something about dogs
Yes! Waiting for a pause and staying on their topic makes it easy to join.
Interrupt: "Guess what! Saturn has rings!"
That is a great fact, but it is a different topic. Join their dog talk first.
Stand behind them without talking for a long time
They might not know you want to join. Wait for a pause, then say something.

situations.s: Talking is like ping-pong. You just asked your friend a question.
o: Your friend
Yes! You hit the ball over. Now it is your friend's turn.
You again
If you keep talking, your friend does not get a turn to answer.
Nobody
Your friend should get a turn to answer.

situations.s: A classmate says "Hi!" to you.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say "Hi!" back (you can wave, too)
Yes! Saying hi back shows you heard them. It is a small, friendly thing.
Walk away without saying anything
They might think you do not like them. A quick "Hi" is enough.
Start telling them about fossils right away
Say hi first. Then you can ask if they want to hear about fossils!

situations.s: Sam puts his toy dinosaur in the RED box and goes outside. While he is gone, Mom moves it to the BLUE box.
o: In the red box
Yes! Sam did not see Mom move it. He only knows what HE saw.
In the blue box
YOU know it is in the blue box, but Sam was outside. He did not see it move.
Under the bed
Sam put it in the red box, so that is where he thinks it is.

situations.s: Mia made you a drawing. You do not really like it.
o: "Thank you for making this for me!"
Yes! You can thank her for her work and kindness. That is true and kind.
"This is ugly."
That might be what you think, but it would hurt her feelings. Thank her for trying.
Throw it away while she watches
That would make her feel very sad. You can say thank you.

situations.s: Your friend's goldfish died. She is crying.
o: "I'm sorry. Do you want to talk or sit together?"
Yes! This shows you care. Right now she needs kindness more than facts.
"Goldfish only live a few years anyway."
It may be true, but it can sound like you do not care. Show kindness first.
Laugh
Laughing when someone is sad can hurt them a lot.

situations.s: Your classmate is scared of spiders. You think spiders are amazing.
o: Keep spider pictures away from them and pick another topic
Yes! Different people like different things. Being kind means respecting that.
Show them lots of spider photos so they stop being scared
That would feel scary for them. Their feelings are real, even if yours are different.
Call them a baby
That is unkind. Everyone is scared of something.

situations.s: Your friend loves horses. You love planets. You are making a birthday card for her.
o: A horse
Yes! A gift is about what the OTHER person likes.
Planets, because you like planets
Planets are great, but the card is for her. Think about what she likes.
Nothing
A card with a horse would make her happy!

situations.s: Tom was not picked for the game. He looks sad.
o: Ask, "Do you want to play with us?"
Yes! Including someone can turn their whole day around.
Pretend you did not see him
He would still feel left out. A small invite helps a lot.
Say, "The team is full forever."
That would make him feel worse. You could invite him.

situations.s: Dad looks outside and says: "It's raining cats and dogs!"
o: It is raining very hard
Yes! It is an idiom. No animals are falling from the sky.
Animals are falling from the sky
That would be amazing, but it is an idiom. It means heavy rain.
Pets are playing in the rain
It is an idiom. It means it is raining very hard.

situations.s: Your brother says: "I'm so hungry I could eat a horse!"
o: He is very, very hungry
Yes! He is not really going to eat a horse. It means VERY hungry.
He wants to eat a horse
It is an idiom. People say it when they are really hungry.
He likes horses
It is an idiom about being really hungry.

situations.s: Before the school play, your friend says: "Break a leg!"
o: Good luck!
Yes! Actors say "break a leg" to mean good luck. Nobody wants you to get hurt.
She wants you to get hurt
It is an idiom. It is a friendly way to say good luck.
Be careful on the stage
It is an idiom that means good luck.

situations.s: You start running to the car. Mom says: "Hold your horses!"
o: Wait a moment
Yes! It means slow down and wait.
Go find some horses
There are no horses. It is an idiom that means wait.
Run faster
It means the opposite: wait a moment.

situations.s: A kid says: "Our teacher has eyes in the back of her head!"
o: The teacher notices a lot
Yes! It means she sees what is going on, even when she is facing the board.
The teacher has extra eyes
People only have two eyes. It is an idiom.
The teacher wears glasses on her head
It is an idiom that means she notices a lot.

situations.s: Your worksheet says: "Circle the -ly adverb."
o: The whole word, like "quietly"
Yes! The adverb is the whole word. "-ly" just tells you how to spot it.
Only the letters "ly"
"ly" is how to find it, but the adverb is the whole word, like "quietly".
Every word in the sentence
Only circle the adverb, the whole -ly word.

situations.s: At dinner, Mom asks: "Can you pass the salt?"
o: Pass her the salt
Yes! It sounds like a question, but it is a polite way to ask you to do it.
Say "Yes, I can" and do nothing
She is not asking IF you can. She is politely asking you to pass it.
Tell her how salt is made
Cool fact! But first pass the salt. That is what she needs.

situations.s: After the spelling test, a friend says: "That was a piece of cake!"
o: The test was easy
Yes! "A piece of cake" means something was easy.
There was cake at the test
It is an idiom. It means easy.
She is hungry for cake
It is an idiom. It means the test was easy.

situations.s: Dad says: "Time to hit the road!"
o: It is time to leave
Yes! "Hit the road" means start a trip or leave.
He will hit the road with his hand
It is an idiom. Nobody hits anything. It means it is time to go.
The road is broken
It is an idiom. It means time to leave.

situations.s: On the first day, the teacher says: "Let's play a game to break the ice."
o: Help everyone feel less shy
Yes! "Break the ice" means help people get to know each other.
Smash some real ice
There is no ice. It is an idiom about feeling less shy.
Make the room colder
It is an idiom about helping people feel comfortable.

situations.s: You lost a board game.
situations.q: What does a good sport do?
o: Say "Good game!"
Yes! Good sports are kind when they win AND when they lose. People will want to play with you again.
Flip the board over
That can scare people. They might not want to play again.
Say "This game is stupid!"
That can hurt the other players' feelings. Try "Good game."

situations.s: You want the swing, but someone is using it.
o: Ask "Can I have a turn when you are done?" and wait
Yes! Asking and waiting is fair. Your turn will come.
Pull them off the swing
That is not safe. Someone could get hurt.
Cry until they get off
Asking with words works better.

situations.s: Your friend wants to play a different game than you.
o: Take turns: her game first, then yours
Yes! Taking turns means you both get to choose.
Only play your game
Your friend would not get a choice. Taking turns is fair.
Go home
You can still have fun together. Try taking turns.

situations.s: Some kids are playing tag. You want to join.
o: "Can I play too?"
Yes! Asking is the clearest way to join.
Grab someone and yell "You're it!"
They might not know you are playing. Ask first.
Wait and hope they ask you
They may not know you want to play. Asking is clearer!

situations.s: Recess is inside because of rain. You wanted to dig for rocks.
situations.q: What is a good Plan B?
o: Draw a rock or read a rock book
Yes! Plan B keeps the fun going. Flexible thinking is a superpower.
Refuse to do anything
That makes recess boring for you. Plan B can still be fun.
Yell at the teacher
The teacher cannot stop the rain. Try a Plan B.

situations.s: Your friend is playing a game with a wrong rule.
o: "I think the rule is... Can we check?"
Yes! Saying it kindly helps everyone. You can check the rules together.
"You're cheating!"
Your friend may just not know the rule. Saying "cheating" can hurt feelings.
Quit the game
You can fix it by talking kindly.

situations.s: A friend is standing very close to your face. You do not like it.
o: "Can you please step back a little?"
Yes! Using words is clear and kind. About one arm's length is a comfy space.
Push them
Pushing can hurt. Use your words.
Scream
Screaming can scare them. A calm sentence works better.

situations.s: You do not understand the math homework.
o: Raise your hand and say "Can you help me with this one?"
Yes! Asking for help is smart. Scientists ask questions all the time.
Rip up the paper
That does not help you learn, and you would lose your work.
Pretend you understand
Then you might stay stuck. Asking helps.

situations.s: Someone is mean to you every day.
o: Tell a grown-up you trust
Yes! This is not a small problem. Grown-ups can help make it stop.
Keep it a secret
Keeping it secret means no one can help you. Tell a grown-up.
Be mean back
That can make the problem bigger. A grown-up can help.

situations.s: You forgot your lunch.
o: Tell your teacher
Yes! Your teacher can help you get food.
Take someone else's lunch
That is not fair to them. Ask a grown-up for help.
Skip lunch and say nothing
Your body needs food. Tell your teacher.

situations.s: The teacher gave 3 steps. You only remember step 1.
o: Ask, "Can you say the steps again?" or look at the board
Yes! Checking is smart. Lots of people forget steps.
Guess the other steps
Guessing can go wrong. It is OK to ask again.
Do nothing
Then you will be stuck. Ask or look at the board.

situations.s: You finished your work early and feel bored.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask the teacher what to do next, or read quietly
Yes! That keeps you busy without bothering others.
Talk loudly to the kids who are still working
They need quiet to finish. Ask the teacher or read.
Walk around the room
That can distract others. Ask the teacher what to do.

situations.s: The noise in the lunchroom is too much for you.
o: Ask a grown-up if you can eat somewhere quieter
Yes! Knowing what your body needs and asking for it is a great skill.
Cover your ears and yell
Covering your ears is OK. Yelling adds more noise, so ask a grown-up for a quieter spot.
Stop eating
Your body needs lunch. Ask for a quieter spot.

situations.s: Ben dropped his ice cream. He is crying.
o: Sad
Yes! Crying is a clue for sad.
Happy
Happy kids often smile. Ben is crying.
Sleepy
Sleepy kids yawn. Ben is crying.

situations.s: Mia got a red balloon. She has a big smile.
o: Happy
Yes! A big smile is a clue for happy.
Sad
Sad kids may cry or look down. Mia is smiling.
Angry
Angry kids may frown or stomp. Mia is smiling.

situations.s: Leo's tower fell down. He frowns and stomps his feet.
o: Mad
Yes! Frowning and stomping are clues for mad.
Happy
Happy kids often smile. Leo is frowning.
Sleepy
Sleepy kids yawn. Leo is stomping.

situations.s: There is a loud boom of thunder. Zoe hides under her blanket.
o: Scared
Yes! Hiding after a loud boom is a clue for scared.
Silly
Silly kids giggle and make funny faces. Zoe is hiding.
Proud
Proud kids stand tall and smile. Zoe is hiding.

situations.s: Noah yawns and rubs his eyes. It is bedtime.
o: Tired
Yes! Yawning and rubbing eyes are clues for tired.
Excited
Excited kids jump and wiggle. Noah is yawning.
Angry
Angry kids may frown or yell. Noah is yawning.

situations.s: It is Priya's first day at a new school. She holds Dad's hand very tight.
o: Nervous
Yes! New places can feel scary. Holding on tight is a clue for nervous.
Silly
Silly kids giggle. Priya is holding on tight.
Bored
Bored kids sigh and look around. Priya is holding on tight.

situations.s: Kai is opening a birthday present. He jumps up and down.
o: Excited
Yes! Jumping up and down is a clue for excited.
Sad
Sad kids may cry or sit still. Kai is jumping.
Scared
Scared kids may hide. Kai is jumping for joy.

situations.s: Omar's dog came home from the vet. Omar grins and flaps his hands.
o: Happy
Yes! Some kids flap their hands when happy. His grin is a clue too.
Scared
Scared kids may hide or freeze. Omar is grinning.
Bored
Bored kids sigh and look away. Omar is grinning.

situations.s: Your crayon broke.
situations.why: Small problem. You can use another crayon.

situations.s: You spilled a little water on the table.
situations.why: Small problem. Get a paper towel and wipe it up.

situations.s: Your shoe came untied.
situations.why: Small problem. Tie it, or ask a grown-up to help.

situations.s: Your tummy hurts a lot at school.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell your teacher so a grown-up can help you.

situations.s: You cannot find your coat at school.
situations.why: Medium problem. Ask your teacher to help you look.

situations.s: Your friend fell off the slide. He is hurt and crying.
situations.why: Big problem. Get a grown-up right away.

situations.s: The fire alarm is ringing.
situations.why: Big problem. Stay calm and follow your teacher right away.

situations.s: One puzzle piece is missing.
situations.q: Which choice fits the size of the problem?
o: Say “Oh well” and keep going
Yes! A small problem gets a small reaction.
Scream and throw the puzzle
That is a big reaction for a small problem. Someone could get hurt.
Say “This is the worst day ever!”
That is a big reaction. One missing piece is a small problem.

situations.s: Your tower fell. You feel very mad.
situations.q: What can help you calm down?
o: Take slow, deep breaths
Yes! Slow breaths help your body calm down. Then the mad gets smaller.
Kick the blocks
Kicking can hurt your foot or break things. The mad feeling stays.
Yell at your friend
Yelling can hurt your friend's feelings. Breathe first.

situations.s: The room is too loud for your ears.
o: Ask for headphones or a quiet spot
Yes! Your ears matter. Asking for quiet is a great tool.
Yell “Stop!” at everyone
Yelling makes more noise. Others may feel upset.
Run away without telling a grown-up
Grown-ups need to know where you are. That keeps you safe.

situations.s: You feel mad at home.
situations.q: What is a safe way to let it out?
o: Squeeze a pillow hard
Yes! Squeezing a pillow is safe. It helps big feelings get smaller.
Throw your toy at the wall
The toy could break, or someone could get hurt.
Hit your brother
Hitting hurts. Your brother would feel sad and scared.

situations.s: You had a hard day. You feel sad.
o: Ask a grown-up for a hug or talk
Yes! Sharing a sad feeling with a grown-up can make it smaller.
Break your crayons
Then your crayons are broken, and you still feel sad.
Hide and tell no one
Sad feelings can grow when we keep them inside. A grown-up can help.

situations.s: It is almost your turn to talk to the class. You feel worried.
o: Count slowly to 5
Yes! Counting slowly helps your body feel calm and ready.
Run out of the room
Your teacher would worry about you. Tell her you feel worried instead.
Keep the worry a secret
Worries can grow inside. Telling a grown-up can help.

situations.s: You ran a lot at recess. Now you feel hot and grumpy.
o: Drink some water and rest
Yes! Water and rest help a hot, tired body feel better.
Take a friend's water without asking
That is not fair to your friend. Ask a grown-up for water.
Stomp and shout at everyone
Shouting can upset others. Your body still feels hot.

situations.s: Your body feels wiggly at circle time.
o: Use a fidget or ask to move
Yes! Some bodies need to move. Asking for a move break is smart.
Poke the kid next to you
Poking can bother or hurt them. Try a fidget instead.
Roll across the rug during the story
Others may not hear the story. Ask for a move break instead.

situations.s: A friend says, “Hi, Mia!”
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say “Hi!” back or wave
Yes! Saying hi or waving shows you heard your friend.
Walk away without a word
Your friend might think you are upset with them. A quick wave is enough.
Start talking about trains right away
Say hi first. Then you can ask if they want to hear about trains!

situations.s: Sam says, “I got a new puppy!”
o: “Cool! What is its name?”
Yes! You asked about Sam's topic. That keeps the talk going.
“I like trucks.”
Trucks are fun, but Sam wants to talk about his puppy.
Say nothing and walk away
Sam might feel ignored. Try asking a question back.

situations.s: Talking is like a ball game. You just asked your friend a question.
o: Your friend
Yes! You sent the ball over. Now it is your friend's turn.
You again
If you keep talking, your friend does not get a turn.
Nobody
Your friend should get a turn to answer.

situations.s: At lunch, Leo asks, “What is your favorite food?”
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Answer, then ask, “What's yours?”
Yes! Answer, then ask back. That keeps the talk going like ping-pong.
Do not answer at all
Leo might think you did not hear him. A short answer is fine.
Talk about your shoes
Leo asked about food. Answer his question first.

situations.s: Rosa is telling you about her cat.
situations.q: How can you show you are listening?
o: Say “Wow!” or ask about her cat
Yes! Words and questions show you are listening. You do not have to look at her.
Walk away while she talks
Rosa might feel sad. She wanted to share with you.
Start singing a loud song
Rosa cannot finish her story. Singing can wait until later.

situations.s: You love dinosaurs. You told Ava lots of dinosaur facts.
o: “Do you want more, or a new topic?”
Yes! Checking lets Ava choose too. Then you both enjoy talking.
Keep going and talk louder
Talking louder does not help Ava enjoy it more. Check with a question.
Stop talking to her forever
You do not need to stop! Just check what Ava wants.

situations.s: Your friend is talking. You think of something fun to say.
o: Hold the idea and wait for a pause
Yes! Waiting lets your friend finish. Then it is your turn.
Talk over your friend
Your friend may feel you did not care about their words.
Shout your idea very loud
Shouting can startle your friend. Wait for a pause instead.

situations.s: You see a bird out the window. Mia is facing the other way.
o: No, she is facing the other way
Yes! People only see what is in front of their eyes.
Yes, she sees what you see
You see the bird, but Mia's eyes point the other way.
She sees two birds
Mia is facing away, so she does not see the bird.

situations.s: Kai puts his cookie in the red box and goes outside. Mom moves it to the blue box.
o: In the red box
Yes! Kai did not see Mom move it. He only knows what he saw.
In the blue box
You know it moved, but Kai was outside. He did not see.
Under the bed
Kai put it in the red box. That is where he thinks it is.

situations.s: Lily made you a picture. You do not love it.
o: “Thank you for making this!”
Yes! Lily worked hard for you. Thanking her is true and kind.
“This is ugly.”
That would hurt Lily's feelings. You can thank her for trying.
Throw it in the trash
Lily would feel very sad. You can say thank you.

situations.s: Zoe loves cats, but you love trucks. You are picking a birthday gift for her.
o: A cat toy
Yes! A gift is about what the other person likes.
A truck toy
Trucks are great, but the gift is for Zoe. She loves cats.
Nothing at all
A cat toy would make Zoe happy!

situations.s: Noah lost his teddy bear. He is sad.
o: Say, “I'm sorry. Can I help look?”
Yes! Helping shows you care about how Noah feels.
Laugh at him
Laughing when someone is sad can hurt a lot.
Say, “It's just a toy.”
It may be just a toy to you, but it matters to Noah.

situations.s: Ava is scared of dogs. Your dog is very friendly.
o: Keep your dog back and let Ava choose
Yes! Ava's feelings are real, even if your dog is nice.
Bring your dog right up to Ava
That could feel very scary for Ava. Let her choose.
Tell Ava she is a baby
That is unkind. Everyone is scared of something.

situations.s: Omar is not in the game. He looks sad.
o: Ask, “Do you want to play?”
Yes! Asking someone to join can make their whole day better.
Pretend you do not see him
Omar would still feel left out. A small invite helps.
Say, “No more players!”
That would make Omar feel even more left out.

situations.s: Balloons keep popping at the party. Ben covers his ears.
o: A quieter spot
Yes! Loud sounds can hurt some ears. A quiet spot can help Ben.
More balloons popping
More pops could hurt Ben's ears even more.
Someone to laugh at him
Laughing would hurt Ben's feelings. His ears need care.

situations.s: Mom is carrying lots of bags. She asks, “Can you give me a hand?”
o: Please help me
Yes! “Give me a hand” means help me. You get to keep your hand!
Give her your hand to keep
Your hand stays with you. It means she wants help.
Clap your hands
No clapping needed. It means she wants help with the bags.

situations.s: The teacher says, “Zip your lips.”
o: Be quiet now
Yes! “Zip your lips” means stop talking for now.
Put a zipper on your mouth
There is no real zipper. It means be quiet.
Zip up your coat
Your coat can stay as it is. It means be quiet.

situations.s: Dad looks outside. He says, “It's raining cats and dogs!”
o: It is raining very hard
Yes! It is a saying. It means lots and lots of rain.
Pets are falling from the sky
No animals are falling! It is a saying for very hard rain.
The dog and cat are wet
It is a saying. It means it is raining very hard.

situations.s: Grandma says, “Shoes on! Hop to it!”
o: Hurry and put your shoes on
Yes! “Hop to it” means start fast. You do not have to hop.
Hop like a bunny
You can hop for fun, but it means hurry up.
Hop to the kitchen
It is a saying. It means get going quickly.

situations.s: You want to tell Grandpa a story. He says, “I'm all ears!”
o: He is ready to listen
Yes! “I'm all ears” means I am ready to listen to you.
He is made of ears
Grandpa looks the same as always. It is a saying.
His ears got very big
His ears did not change. It means he wants to listen.

situations.s: The teacher says, “Line up for lunch!”
o: Stand in a line by the door
Yes! “Line up” means stand one behind the other.
Draw a line on your paper
It is not about drawing. It means stand in a line.
Lie down on the floor
“Line up” means stand in a line, not lie down.

situations.s: You start running to the car. Mom says, “Hold your horses!”
o: Wait a moment
Yes! “Hold your horses” means slow down and wait.
Go find some horses
There are no horses. It is a saying that means wait.
Run faster
It means the opposite. Slow down and wait.

situations.s: At the doctor, the nurse says, “Please take a seat.”
o: Sit down in a chair
Yes! “Take a seat” means sit down.
Carry a chair away
You do not carry the chair. It means sit down.
Take a chair home
The chair stays there. It means sit down.

situations.s: You want the swing. Someone else is on it.
o: Ask, “Can I have a turn next?”
Yes! Asking and waiting is fair. Your turn will come.
Pull them off the swing
That is not safe. Someone could get hurt.
Yell, “Get off now!”
Yelling can scare them. Asking with a calm voice works better.

situations.s: Some kids are playing tag. You want to play too.
o: “Can I play too?”
Yes! Asking is the clearest way to join a game.
Grab a kid and yell “You're it!”
They may not know you are playing. Ask first.
Say nothing and watch from far away
They may not know you want to play. You can ask!

situations.s: You lost a board game.
situations.q: What does a good sport do?
o: Say “Good game!”
Yes! Good sports are kind when they lose. Friends will want to play again.
Throw the game pieces
Pieces could hit someone. Friends may not want to play again.
Say “You cheated!”
That can hurt your friend's feelings. Try saying “Good game.”

situations.s: You won the race at recess!
situations.q: What does a good sport do?
o: Say “Good race!” to the others
Yes! Good sports are kind when they win, too.
Shout “You lose!” over and over
The other kids may feel sad. They might not race again.
Dance right in their faces
Happy dances are fun, but not in their faces. They may feel sad.

situations.s: The park trip is off because of rain. You feel let down.
situations.q: What is a good Plan B?
o: Build a blanket fort inside
Yes! Plan B keeps the fun going. It is OK to feel let down first.
Say “No fun ever again!”
Rain can't stop all the fun. A Plan B can still be fun.
Stand by the door all day
The rain may not stop soon. Plan B can be fun too.

situations.s: A friend is standing very close to you. You do not like it.
o: “Please step back a little.”
Yes! Words are clear and kind. Your body space matters.
Push your friend
Pushing can hurt. Use your words instead.
Scream at your friend
Screaming can scare your friend. Calm words work better.

situations.s: Mia wants to play blocks. You want to play trains.
o: Blocks first, then trains
Yes! Taking turns means you both get to choose.
Only play trains
Mia would not get a choice. Taking turns is fair.
Grab the blocks away
Grabbing is not fair. Mia may feel upset.

situations.s: Leo wants your toy car. You are not done yet.
o: “You can have it when I'm done.”
Yes! You finish your turn, and Leo knows he gets one next.
Hit Leo
Hitting hurts. Leo would feel sad and scared.
Hide the car forever
Leo would never get a turn. That is not fair.

situations.s: At lunch, you cannot open your milk.
o: Ask, “Can you help me open this?”
Yes! Asking for help is smart. Grown-ups like to help.
Throw it on the floor
It could spill, and you still have no milk.
Give up and drink nothing
Your body needs a drink. Asking for help is OK.

situations.s: You are at the store. You cannot see your grown-up.
o: Ask a worker or a parent with kids
Yes! Store workers and parents with kids can help you find your grown-up.
Walk out to the parking lot
Outside has cars. Stay inside so your grown-up can find you.
Hide in the clothes rack
Your grown-up cannot find you if you hide. Ask a worker for help.

situations.s: A big kid pushes you at recess every day.
o: Tell a grown-up you trust
Yes! When someone hurts you, tell a grown-up. They can help it stop.
Keep it a secret
If you keep it secret, no one can help you.
Push back harder
Someone could get hurt, and the problem gets bigger. Tell a grown-up.

situations.s: At the park, a grown-up you do not know walks up. They say, “Come see my puppy.”
o: Say “No” and go to your grown-up
Yes! Always stay with your grown-up. Tell them what happened.
Go with them to see the puppy
Always ask your own grown-up first. Stay where they can see you.
Keep it a secret
Your grown-up wants to know. Telling them keeps you safe.

situations.s: The teacher told the class what to do. You do not know what to do.
o: Ask, “Can you say it again?”
Yes! Lots of kids need to hear it again. Asking is smart.
Guess and hope it is right
Guessing can go wrong. It is OK to ask.
Sit and do nothing
Then you stay stuck. Asking helps you get started.

situations.s: The party is too loud for you.
o: Tell a grown-up, “I need a quiet break.”
Yes! Knowing what your body needs and asking for it is a great skill.
Scream louder than the noise
Screaming adds more noise. A grown-up can help you find quiet.
Hide and tell no one
Your grown-up may worry. Tell them, and they can help.

situations.s: You are at the doctor. You feel scared about a shot.
o: Tell your grown-up, “I feel scared.”
Yes! Saying your feeling helps. A grown-up can hold your hand.
Kick the doctor
Kicking hurts. The doctor is there to help you stay healthy.
Run out the door
Your grown-up needs to know where you are. Tell them how you feel.

situations.s: You need to use the bathroom during class.
o: Raise your hand and ask to go
Yes! Asking lets your teacher know where you are.
Walk out without telling anyone
Your teacher would not know where you are. Ask first.
Wait and wait until it hurts
Waiting too long is hard on your body. It is OK to ask.

situations.s: Aisha finished a big puzzle. She sits up tall and smiles.
o: Proud
Yes! Sitting tall and smiling after hard work are clues for proud.
Sad
Sad kids may cry or look down. Aisha is smiling.
Scared
Scared kids may hide or freeze. Aisha is sitting tall.

situations.s: Mom said no candy at the store. Mateo crosses his arms and pouts.
o: Upset
Yes! Crossed arms and a pout are clues for upset. He wanted candy.
Happy
Happy kids often smile. Mateo is pouting.
Sleepy
Sleepy kids yawn. Mateo has crossed arms.

situations.s: Hana sees Grandma at the bus stop. She waves fast and laughs.
o: Happy
Yes! Waving and laughing are clues for happy. She loves Grandma!
Angry
Angry kids may frown or stomp. Hana is laughing.
Bored
Bored kids sigh and look away. Hana is waving fast.

situations.s: Dev opens the door. His cousins yell, “Surprise!” His mouth opens wide.
o: Surprised
Yes! A wide-open mouth is a clue for surprised. He did not know!
Tired
Tired kids yawn and move slowly. Dev's mouth popped open.
Bored
Bored kids sigh. Something new just happened to Dev.

situations.s: Ling gets a new worksheet. She tilts her head. She scratches her head.
o: Confused
Yes! Tilting and scratching your head are clues for confused. She could ask for help.
Excited
Excited kids jump and smile. Ling is scratching her head.
Angry
Angry kids may frown or stomp. Ling is tilting her head.

situations.s: Tomás rocks in his favorite chair. He hums softly. His body is slow.
o: Calm
Yes! Soft humming and slow rocking are clues for calm. Rocking helps some kids feel good.
Mad
Mad kids may frown or stomp. Tomás is humming softly.
Scared
Scared kids may hide. Tomás is relaxed in his chair.

situations.s: Chloe trips in the lunch line. Her cheeks turn pink. She covers her face.
o: Embarrassed
Yes! Pink cheeks and hiding your face are clues for embarrassed. Everyone trips sometimes.
Proud
Proud kids stand tall and smile. Chloe is hiding her face.
Sleepy
Sleepy kids yawn. Chloe has pink cheeks.

situations.s: Your favorite show is over.
situations.why: Small problem. It can feel sad for a moment. You can watch it another day.

situations.s: You wanted the green cup. You got a blue cup.
situations.why: Small problem. The blue cup holds your drink too. You can ask for green next time.

situations.s: You left your jacket at the park.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell a grown-up. You can go back and look together, or check the lost and found.

situations.s: Your little brother drew on your homework.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell a grown-up. They can help you fix it or tell your teacher.

situations.s: Grandpa fell down at home. He cannot get up.
situations.why: Big problem. Stay calm and get another grown-up right away. If no other grown-up is there, call 911.

situations.s: You see a little kid walking into the street alone.
situations.why: Big problem. Call a grown-up right away so they can keep the kid safe. Stay on the sidewalk yourself.

situations.s: You wanted to be first in line. You are third.
situations.q: Which choice fits the size of the problem?
o: Take a breath. Third is okay.
Yes! A small problem gets a small reaction. You still get to go.
Push to the front
Pushing can hurt someone. That is a big reaction for a small problem.
Yell “No fair!” over and over
That is a big reaction. The whole line gets there together.

situations.s: The tag in your shirt feels itchy. It bugs you a lot.
o: Tell a grown-up. Ask to cut the tag or change shirts.
Yes! Itchy clothes can feel awful. Asking for help is a great tool.
Rip your shirt
Then your shirt is broken. A grown-up can help in a safer way.
Say nothing and feel worse all day
It is okay to speak up. Your body matters.

situations.s: The store is bright and busy. Your body feels too full.
o: Ask for your hat, headphones or a break outside
Yes! Bright, busy places can be a lot. A break helps your body reset.
Knock things off the shelf
Things could break. Your grown-up would need to stop and clean up.
Run away down the aisle
Your grown-up needs to know where you are. That keeps you safe.

situations.s: You feel worried on the bus. Your hands want to move.
o: Squeeze a fidget or flap your hands
Yes! Moving your hands can help you feel calm. That is okay to do.
Poke the kid next to you
Poking can bother or hurt the other kid. Keep moves on your own body.
Stand up while the bus moves
Standing on a moving bus is not safe. Stay in your seat.

situations.s: Your teacher is out today. There is a new teacher. You feel upset.
o: Ask, “What is the plan today?”
Yes! Knowing the plan helps changes feel less scary. Your teacher will be back.
Hide under the table all day
You would miss the fun. Asking about the plan can help you feel safe.
Yell at the new teacher
The new teacher may feel sad. It is not their fault your teacher is out.

situations.s: You are drawing a cat. It does not look right. You feel frustrated.
o: Take a short break, then try again
Yes! A break helps your brain reset. Then try again.
Rip up the paper
Then your drawing is gone. A break is a better tool.
Say, “I am bad at everything”
That is not true! Everyone makes mistakes. Be kind to yourself.

situations.s: At Auntie's house, the food smells too strong for you.
o: Quietly ask to sit in another room for a bit
Yes! It is okay to need a break. Asking quietly is kind to Auntie.
Say, “Yuck! It stinks!”
Auntie worked hard to cook. Those words could hurt her feelings.
Hold it in until you cry
Holding it in can make it worse. It is okay to ask for a break.

situations.s: It is dark at bedtime. You feel scared.
o: Ask for a night-light or a hug
Yes! A little light or a hug can help you feel safe.
Scream as loud as you can
Screaming can scare your family. You can call or walk to a grown-up.
Stay scared and tell no one
A grown-up can help. You do not have to feel scared alone.

situations.s: Grandma asks, “How was school?”
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Tell her one thing you did
Yes! One thing is enough. Grandma likes hearing about your day.
Walk away without a word
Grandma may feel sad. She wants to know about your day.
Talk about your video game
That is a new topic. Answer Grandma's question first.

situations.s: Your friend Sofia says, “Bye! See you tomorrow!”
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say “Bye!” or wave
Yes! Saying bye or waving shows Sofia you heard her.
Keep playing and say nothing
Sofia may think you did not hear her. A quick wave is enough.
Start a long story about trains
Sofia is leaving now. You can tell her tomorrow!

situations.s: Mom is talking on the phone. You want to ask her something.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Put your hand on her arm and wait
Yes! That tells Mom you need her. She can answer when her call is done.
Yell your question loud
The person on the phone cannot hear Mom. Mom may feel upset.
Pull the phone away
That would stop Mom's talk. It is her turn right now.

situations.s: Mr. Kim asks you a question. You did not hear it.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say, “Can you say that again, please?”
Yes! Asking again is smart. Grown-ups are happy to repeat.
Just guess an answer
Your guess may not match his question. Asking again works better.
Say nothing
Mr. Kim may wait and wait. A few words help him know.

situations.s: Yuki asks, “Do you have a pet?” You say, “Yes, a fish.”
o: “Do you have a pet?”
Yes! Asking back sends the ball over. Now Yuki gets a turn.
Walk away
Yuki may feel sad. The talk was just getting started.
“Fish are the best pets. Yours is not as good.”
Yuki may feel hurt. Asking about her pet is kinder.

situations.s: You and Liam are talking about soccer. You want to talk about space.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask, “Can I tell you about space now?”
Yes! Asking first is a kind way to change the topic.
Start talking about space right away
Liam may feel confused. He was still thinking about soccer.
Stop talking to Liam
Liam may think you are upset. You can just ask to switch.

situations.s: Your neighbor Mrs. Lopez says, “Good morning!” Looking at faces is hard for you.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say “Good morning!” or wave
Yes! That shows you heard her. You can look wherever feels okay.
Say nothing
Mrs. Lopez may think you did not hear her. A wave works too.
Run inside fast
Mrs. Lopez may feel sad. A quick hi or wave is enough.

situations.s: You tell a joke about Ana's hat. Ana does not laugh. She looks down.
o: The joke hurt her feelings
Yes! Looking down is a clue. You could say, “Sorry. I did not mean to hurt you.”
The joke was very funny
Kids who think a joke is funny usually laugh. Ana is looking down.
She wants another joke about her hat
Ana looks sad. Another joke may make her feel worse.

situations.s: Your sister is reading a book. You want to play loud music.
o: Quiet time to read
Yes! Reading is easier when it is quiet. You could use headphones or play in another room.
To dance with you
She is busy reading. You could ask her later.
To go to bed
She is reading, not sleeping. She just wants quiet.

situations.s: Your family is planning a surprise party for Grandpa. Nobody told Grandpa.
o: It is a normal day
Yes! Grandpa was not told. People only know what they see or hear.
There is a party today
Grandpa was not told. He cannot know yet. That is the surprise!

situations.s: Aria shows you her new shoes. She keeps pointing at them.
o: For you to notice and say something nice
Yes! Pointing is a clue. She is proud and wants to share.
For you to take her shoes
They are her shoes. She wants to show them, not give them.
For you to leave
Aria is sharing with you. She wants you to stay and look.

situations.s: Kofi is playing at your house. He yawns and keeps looking at the door.
o: To rest or go home soon
Yes! Yawning and looking at the door are clues. You could ask, “Are you tired?”
To play for many more hours
Yawning is a clue for tired, not for more play.
To be mad at you
Kofi is not frowning. He looks tired.

situations.s: You love spicy food. Wei tries some. He drinks lots of water fast.
situations.q: What does Wei think of the food?
o: It is too spicy for him
Yes! Drinking water fast is a clue. People can like different things.
He loves it just like you
Wei might not like what you like. Look at the water clue.
He is bored
Bored kids sigh. Wei is gulping water.

situations.s: Isabella is building with blocks. She says, “Please don't touch. I have a plan.”
o: To build it her own way
Yes! She told you her plan. You could build your own tower next to her.
Help moving the blocks
She said, “Please don't touch.” That means she wants to do it herself.
To knock it down
She has a plan to build. Knocking it down would make her sad.

situations.s: You are buckled in the car. Mom says, “Sit tight. We are almost there!”
o: Stay in your seat and wait a little longer
Yes! “Sit tight” means stay where you are and wait. The ride is almost over.
Squeeze your body very tight
No squeezing needed! It is a saying. It means stay put and wait.
Get out of the car now
The car is still going. “Sit tight” means stay in your seat.

situations.s: Grandpa hugs you. He says, “You are the apple of my eye.”
o: He loves you very much
Yes! It means you are very special to him.
There is an apple in his eye
There is no real apple. It is a saying that means love.
He wants an apple
He is not asking for a snack. He is saying you are special.

situations.s: The teacher says, “Put on your listening ears.”
o: Get ready to listen
Yes! It means be ready to hear what comes next. You can listen in your own way.
Find new ears to put on
That is a funny picture! It means get ready to listen.
Cover your ears
Covering your ears is okay if it is too loud. But she means get ready to listen.

situations.s: You are stuck on a hard puzzle. Mom says, “Hang in there!”
o: Keep trying. Do not give up.
Yes! “Hang in there” means keep going when something is hard. You can take a break and come back too.
Hang from the monkey bars
No hanging needed! It is a saying. It means keep trying.
Hang the puzzle on the wall
The puzzle can stay on the table. It means keep trying.

situations.s: It is late. Dad yawns and says, “Time to hit the hay!”
o: It is time to go to bed
Yes! “Hit the hay” means go to sleep. Long ago, some beds were stuffed with hay.
Hit a pile of hay
No hitting! It is a saying. It means bedtime.
Go feed the horses
There are no horses here. It means it is time to sleep.

situations.s: At soccer, Coach says, “Keep your eye on the ball!”
o: Watch where the ball goes
Yes! It means pay attention to the ball.
Put your eye on top of the ball
That would be silly! It means watch the ball.
Hold the ball near your face
It is a saying. It means keep watching the ball.

situations.s: You are painting with Grandma. She says, “Let's call it a day.”
o: We are done for today
Yes! “Call it a day” means stop for now. You can paint again later.
Say the word “day” out loud
No need to call anything. It means stop for now.
Give the day a new name
Days keep their names! It means we are done.

situations.s: Kids are taking turns on the slide. You want to go again right away.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Get back in line
Yes! Waiting in line is fair. Everyone gets a turn.
Cut to the front
Others were waiting too. Cutting feels unfair to them.
Stay at the top and not slide
Kids behind you are waiting. Slide down so they get a turn.

situations.s: At the park, Diego's ball rolls over to you.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Roll or toss it back to him
Yes! It is his ball. Giving it back is kind and fair.
Keep it and walk away
Diego may feel sad and worried. It is his ball.
Kick it far away
Diego would have to chase it. He may think you are being mean.

situations.s: You and Eli both grab the same ball at recess.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say, “Let's take turns.”
Yes! Taking turns means you both get to play.
Pull as hard as you can
Someone could fall and get hurt. Talking works better.
Yell “Mine!”
Yelling can upset Eli. The ball is for everyone.

situations.s: Your friends want new rules for the game. You like the old rules.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say how you feel. Then try the new rules or pick a new game.
Yes! Your feelings matter. Trying new rules can be fun too.
Quit and yell “You're doing it wrong!”
Your friends may feel sad. There can be more than one way to play.
Play but keep using the old rules
Then the game gets mixed up. It helps to all play the same way.

situations.s: You are playing with friends. You feel tired. You want to be alone.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say, “I need a break. I will play later.”
Yes! Taking a break is okay. Telling friends helps them understand.
Walk away without a word
Friends may think you are mad at them. A few words help.
Yell “Go away!”
Your friends may feel hurt. You can ask for a break kindly.

situations.s: In a race, Nora trips and falls. Some kids laugh.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask Nora, “Are you okay?”
Yes! Nora may feel hurt or embarrassed. A kind word helps.
Laugh too
Laughing can make Nora feel worse. Falls are not funny to the one who fell.
Keep running and do not look back
Nora may need help. Checking on her is kind.

situations.s: On the bus, you want to sit with Grace. She says, “I'm saving this seat for Lucy.”
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say “Okay” and find another seat
Yes! Grace made a plan with Lucy. You can sit with Grace another day.
Sit there anyway
Grace told you it is saved. Sitting there could upset her and Lucy.
Say, “You're not my friend!”
That could hurt Grace's feelings. She can still be your friend.

situations.s: Your cup is on a high shelf at home. You cannot reach it.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask a grown-up to get it
Yes! Asking for help keeps you safe.
Climb up the shelf
Shelves are not for climbing. You could fall.
Cry and give up
It is okay to feel upset. But a grown-up can help you fast.

situations.s: Your zipper is stuck. Everyone is going outside.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Say, “Can you help me with my zipper?”
Yes! Asking a grown-up or a friend is a smart move.
Stay inside by yourself
You would miss recess. And grown-ups need to know where you are.
Pull and pull until it breaks
Then your coat is broken. Asking for help is faster.

situations.s: At the library, you cannot find a book about sharks.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask the librarian for help
Yes! Helping people find books is the librarian's job.
Pull all the books off the shelf
That makes a big mess. The librarian can find it faster.
Give up and go home
You do not have to give up. A helper is right there.

situations.s: Mei drops her box of crayons. They roll everywhere.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask, “Do you want help?” Then help pick them up.
Yes! Asking first is kind. Many hands make the job quick.
Laugh at the mess
Mei may feel embarrassed. Everyone drops things sometimes.
Take some crayons for you
Those are Mei's crayons. Taking them is not fair.

situations.s: A word on your worksheet is too hard to read.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Raise your hand and ask for help
Yes! Asking for help is how we learn. Teachers are glad to help.
Scribble on the page
Scribbling will not help you read the word. Ask instead.
Copy your neighbor's paper
That is your neighbor's work. Your teacher wants to help you learn.

situations.s: You feel sick on the school bus.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Tell the bus driver
Yes! The bus driver is the grown-up in charge. They can help you.
Say nothing
A grown-up cannot help if they do not know. It is okay to tell.
Walk around the bus
Walking on a moving bus is not safe. Stay in your seat and tell the driver.

situations.s: Carlos is crying on the bench. You do not know why.
situations.q: What is a good thing to do?
o: Ask, “Are you okay? Want me to get a teacher?”
Yes! Asking shows you care. Carlos can choose what he needs.
Laugh at him
Laughing can make Carlos feel worse. Crying is okay.
Ignore him
Carlos might feel alone. A kind question can help.

situations.s: Diego's group is presenting their poster next. He keeps tapping his foot and reading his notecard again and again.
o: Nervous about presenting
Yes! Tapping and rereading are clues for nervous. Lots of people feel this before speaking to a group.
Bored with the poster
Bored people often slump or look away. Diego is busy checking his notes.
Angry at his group
Angry clues are frowns or sharp words. Diego is quiet and focused on his card.

situations.s: You text Aisha a long message about your weekend. She replies with just "ok."
situations.q: What is the best way to figure out how she feels?
o: Remember texts hide faces, so ask: "Is now a good time?"
Yes! A short text can mean busy, not upset. Asking gently clears it up.
Decide she is mad at you
"ok" might just mean she is in the middle of dinner. Guessing "mad" can worry you for no reason.
Send ten more messages right away
Lots of messages at once can feel like a lot. Give her time to answer.

situations.s: Mateo got his math test back. He folded it fast, shoved it in his desk, and crossed his arms.
o: Disappointed or embarrassed about his score
Yes! Hiding the paper and crossed arms are clues. He may not want to talk yet.
Proud of his score
Proud people often show their paper or smile. Mateo hid his.
Sleepy
Sleepy people yawn and move slowly. Mateo moved fast and crossed his arms.

situations.s: At lunch, Hana says "I'm fine" in a flat voice. She is not eating and stares at her tray.
o: Her words say fine, but her body clues say something is wrong
Yes! Sometimes words and body clues do not match. You could say, "I'm here if you want to talk."
She is definitely fine because she said so
People sometimes say "fine" when they are not. Her other clues tell more of the story.
She is angry at you
Her clues show she feels down. There is no sign it is about you.

situations.s: Kofi's team lost the championship. He is smiling and clapping for the other team, but his eyes look wet.
o: Sad, and also trying to be a good sport
Yes! People can feel two things at once. He is sad and still being kind.
Only happy
His smile is real kindness, but wet eyes are a clue for sadness too.
Scared
Scared clues are wide eyes or freezing. Kofi is clapping and a little teary.

situations.s: You tell Ruby about your fossil collection. She leans in, asks "Wait, how old is that one?" and grins.
situations.q: What do her clues tell you?
o: She is interested and wants to hear more
Yes! Leaning in and asking questions are clues for interested. Enjoy sharing!
She wants you to stop talking
People ready to stop often look away or change the topic. Ruby asked a question.
She is confused and upset
A question with a grin shows curiosity, not upset.

situations.s: Noah dropped his spaghetti tray in the cafeteria. His cheeks turned pink and he looked at the floor.
o: Embarrassed
Yes! Pink cheeks and looking down are clues for embarrassed. A kind helper can make it better.
Excited
Excited people bounce and smile big. Noah is looking at the floor.
Proud
Proud people stand tall. Noah looks like he wants to hide.

situations.s: Your online game freezes and you lose ten minutes of progress.
situations.why: Small problem. It is annoying, but you can take a breath and play that part again.

situations.s: There is a substitute teacher today, and the schedule is a little different.
situations.why: Small problem. Changes can feel strange. You can ask the sub, "What are we doing next?"

situations.s: Your group project partner has not done his part, and it is due tomorrow.
situations.why: Medium problem. Talk to your partner first. If that does not work, tell your teacher today.

situations.s: You left your backpack on the bus with your library book inside.
situations.why: Medium problem. Tell a grown-up at school so they can call the bus office.

situations.s: Someone in an online game chat asks for your home address.
situations.why: Big problem, and you know what to do. Do not answer. Tell a trusted grown-up right away. You are not in trouble. Private info like your address stays private.

situations.s: Your friend at the lunch table has a peanut allergy and starts having trouble breathing.
situations.why: Big problem. Tell the nearest grown-up right away. Grown-ups know how to help with allergies fast. If no grown-up is there, call 911.

situations.s: You find out your book report is due Friday, not next week. It is Wednesday.
situations.q: Which reaction matches the size of the problem?
o: Make a plan: read tonight, write tomorrow, ask for help if stuck
Yes! A medium problem gets a plan. Breaking it into small steps makes it doable.
Rip up the book and say you quit
That is a big reaction. Tearing things up adds a new problem.
Ignore it and hope it goes away
Ignoring a medium problem can make it bigger. A plan helps it shrink.

situations.s: At a school assembly, the microphone squeals and the lights are bright. Your body feels buzzy.
o: Use your headphones or ask your teacher for a quick break
Yes! Protecting your senses is smart. Asking for a break is a strong, brave tool.
Push through and pretend you are fine
Hiding big feelings can make them grow. It is okay to take care of your body.
Scream so the noise stops
Screaming adds more noise and may scare others. Try a tool that helps you.

situations.s: You were explaining your idea, and a classmate talked over you. You feel your face get hot.
situations.q: What is a good first step?
o: Take a slow breath, then say "I wasn't finished yet"
Yes! A breath helps you stay calm. Then you can speak up in a clear, kind way.
Shout louder until he stops
Shouting can turn into an argument. Calm words work better.
Stop talking and never share ideas again
Your ideas matter! One interruption does not mean you should stop sharing.

situations.s: During a long test, your hands want to flap and your leg keeps bouncing.
o: Use a quiet fidget or squeeze your hands under the desk
Yes! Moving helps many brains focus, and flapping is okay. During a test, a quiet move lets you and others keep working.
Tell yourself moving is bad and freeze
Movement is not bad. Your body may need it to think.
Get up and walk around the room during the test
Walking around can distract others during a test. Ask first, or try a quiet move.

situations.s: You are at a sleepover. It is late, the room is new, and you feel homesick and wobbly.
o: Tell the grown-up there how you feel and ask to call home
Yes! Many kids feel homesick. Grown-ups can help, and a call can calm you down.
Hide under the blanket and cry alone all night
You do not have to handle it alone. Telling someone is brave.
Sneak out to walk home
Leaving without telling a grown-up is not safe. Ask for help instead.

situations.s: Your computer project will not save, and you have tried three times. You want to slam the laptop.
situations.q: What is a good calm-down move?
o: Step away, count to ten, then ask for tech help
Yes! A short break cools your brain. Then a helper can fix the tech problem.
Slam the laptop shut
Slamming could break the computer and lose your work for real.
Keep clicking save faster and faster
Clicking faster usually does not fix it. A break and help work better.

situations.s: Your thoughts are racing about tomorrow's field day. What if you do not know the rules?
o: Ask your teacher for the schedule and rules ahead of time
Yes! Knowing what to expect can shrink worried feelings. Planning is a great tool.
Stay up all night worrying
Worry grows when you are tired. Getting information helps more.
Decide to fake being sick
Fake sick means you miss the fun. Getting the facts can make it feel doable.

situations.s: Priyanka feels her anger rising in gym class. Her teacher lets kids use a calm corner.
situations.q: What is a good choice for Priyanka?
o: Go to the calm corner and take some deep breaths
Yes! Using the calm corner is a smart, grown-up choice. She can join again when ready.
Kick the ball as hard as she can at the wall
That could hurt someone or break something. A calm tool is safer.
Yell at the kid closest to her
That kid did not cause her feelings. Yelling could hurt them.

situations.s: You have been talking about train engines for ten minutes. Your friend Omar keeps saying "uh-huh."
situations.q: What is a good next move?
o: Ask Omar, "What have you been into lately?"
Yes! Short answers can mean it's his turn. Asking about him keeps the ping-pong going.
Keep going. There are more engine facts
Your facts are cool! But conversations work best when both people get turns.
Walk away because he is not interested
He may still like you a lot. He might just want a turn to talk.

situations.s: At the lunch table, four kids are talking about a movie you have not seen.
situations.q: What could you say to join in?
o: "I haven't seen it. What's it about?"
Yes! Asking a question is a great way to join. People like sharing about things they enjoy.
Start talking about your favorite video game
Switching topics suddenly can feel confusing. Join their topic first.
Say "That movie sounds dumb"
That could hurt their feelings. A question is kinder and helps you join.

situations.s: Lucía is telling a story. You just remembered something important you want to add.
o: Hold the thought and wait until she finishes
Yes! Waiting shows respect. You can squeeze your hand to help remember your idea.
Say it right now, in the middle of her sentence
Interrupting can make someone feel their story does not matter.
Forget about it and never say it
Your idea still matters. You can share it when she is done.

situations.s: Your friend Jin texts you: "I got a new puppy!!"
situations.q: Which reply keeps the conversation going?
o: "No way! What's its name?"
Yes! Showing interest and asking a question keeps the ping-pong going.
"ok"
A one-word reply can feel like you do not care. Add a question or a feeling.
"I got a new video game today"
Jumping to your own news can feel like you skipped his. Respond to his news first.

situations.s: In an online game chat, a teammate types "gg" after your team loses.
o: "gg, that was fun!"
Yes! "gg" means "good game." Saying it back is friendly game manners.
"You were terrible"
Mean chat hurts real people. Kind words keep the game fun for everyone.
Type in all capital letters about how mad you are
All caps can feel like yelling in chat. Take a break if you feel upset.

situations.s: A new student, Amara, sits by you. She is quiet and looking around.
situations.q: What is a friendly way to start?
o: "Hi! I like the drawing on your notebook. Do you like art?"
Yes! A hello and a question about something you noticed is a great opener.
Say nothing and wait for her to talk
That is okay if you need quiet. But a small hello can help her feel welcome.
Ask her lots of questions all at once
Many questions quickly can feel like a lot. One question at a time works better.

situations.s: You asked Ethan a question. He is thinking, and it has been a few seconds.
o: Wait a little longer for him to answer
Yes! Some people need more time to think. Waiting is kind.
Ask the same question again, louder
Repeating louder can feel like pressure. Give him time.
Answer the question for him
Answering for him takes away his turn. Let him share his own answer.

situations.s: There is a substitute teacher. She does not know the class usually gets five minutes of free reading.
situations.q: Why might she say no to free reading?
o: She does not know your class's routine
Yes! People only know what they have been told. You could politely explain the routine.
She is being mean on purpose
She probably just does not know. Most subs want the day to go well.
She knows but wants to trick you
Subs usually follow the plan they were given. She likely just did not see it.

situations.s: Your friend Wei gives you a book about bugs. You already have that exact book.
o: He picked something he thought you would love
Yes! He knew you like bugs and wanted to make you happy. You could say "Thanks, I love bugs!"
He wanted to give you something you already had
He did not know you had it. His brain did not have that information.
He does not care about you
Choosing a gift about your interest shows he does care.

situations.s: You know everything about octopus camouflage. Your partner Jada has never heard of it.
situations.q: What should you remember when you explain it?
o: Jada does not know what you know, so start simple
Yes! Other people's brains have different facts. Starting simple helps her follow along.
Jada already knows all of it
She said she has never heard of it. Her brain has different information.
Jada will not be interested at all
She might be very interested! Explaining it clearly gives her a chance to enjoy it.

situations.s: You laughed when Carlos tripped, because it looked funny. Now Carlos looks upset.
o: "They are laughing at me. That hurts."
Yes! Even if you did not mean it, laughing can feel mean to the person who fell. You could say sorry.
"That was funny, I'm glad they laughed"
His upset face is a clue that he did not find it funny.
He is not thinking about it at all
His face shows he noticed. Checking in can help.

situations.s: At a sleepover, you want pizza with pineapple. Your friend's family ordered plain cheese.
situations.q: What is a good way to think about it?
o: They do not know your favorite, and cheese is still food you can eat
Yes! Hosts cannot read minds. You could eat what works for you, and say thanks.
They ordered cheese to upset you
They probably just ordered what they usually get. It was not about you.
You should refuse to eat anything
Hosts may worry if you do not eat. It is fine to eat what you like from what is there.

situations.s: In your group project, Zoe keeps adding purple to the poster. You wanted blue.
o: She likes purple and may not know you wanted blue
Yes! You could say, "Can we use blue for the title?" Talking helps you share ideas.
She is trying to ruin the poster
She is probably just adding colors she likes. She may not know your plan.
She knows exactly what you wanted
People cannot read minds. Say your idea out loud so she knows.

situations.s: Your classmate Dev always wears headphones in the cafeteria. A kid asks you, "Why is he so weird?"
o: "Maybe loud places hurt his ears. Headphones help lots of people."
Yes! Different people need different things. Helping others understand is kind.
"Yeah, he is weird"
Agreeing could hurt Dev's feelings. Wearing headphones is a smart way to take care of himself.
Say nothing and laugh
Laughing can join in the teasing. A kind explanation helps more.

situations.s: It is pouring rain on field day. Your friend says, "Oh great, perfect weather."
o: The weather is bad. She is being sarcastic.
Yes! Sarcasm says the opposite of what you mean. Her tone and the rain are clues.
She thinks the rain is perfect
The words say "perfect," but rain on field day is a clue. She means the opposite.
She wants you to go get an umbrella
She is sharing a feeling, not asking for anything.

situations.s: Your teacher says, "Let's put our heads together on this problem."
o: Let's work on it as a team and share ideas
Yes! "Put our heads together" means think together. No real heads touching!
Everyone should touch foreheads
This is a figure of speech. It is about sharing thoughts, not heads.
Put your head down on the desk
This phrase means team thinking, not resting.

situations.s: Before the spelling bee, Maya says, "I'm getting cold feet."
o: She feels nervous and is thinking about not doing it
Yes! "Cold feet" means feeling nervous before something big. You could say, "You'll do great!"
Her feet are actually cold
This is a figure of speech. It is about a nervous feeling.
She wants to put on socks
Maya is talking about feelings, not socks.

situations.s: Your friend tells a joke: "Why did the math book look sad? It had too many problems!"
o: "Problems" means math problems and also troubles
Yes! Many jokes use a word with two meanings. That's called a pun.
Math books really feel sad
Books don't have feelings. The joke plays with a word's two meanings.
It is not a joke, it is a fact
It is a joke. The fun part is the word "problems."

situations.s: You tell a classmate you got a new pencil case. He says, "Wow. Big news." in a flat voice.
o: He might be teasing that it is not a big deal
Yes! A flat voice with "wow" can be sarcasm. You can shrug it off or say "I like it!"
He thinks it is huge, amazing news
His flat voice is a clue. People who are excited sound bouncy and loud.
He wants to borrow your pencil case
He did not ask to borrow anything. Listen to his tone.

situations.s: Your coach says, "Let's hit the ground running today."
o: Let's start fast and with lots of energy
Yes! It means get started quickly and eagerly. You do not have to hit the ground.
Hit the ground with your hands while you run
This is an idiom. It means start strong, not hit anything.
Only run today, no other drills
The coach means start with energy. It is not about the plan for practice.

situations.s: In a group text, Aaliyah writes "lol you're so weird 😜" after your joke.
o: She is joking in a friendly way
Yes! The laughing "lol" and silly emoji are clues she means it kindly.
She thinks you are bad
Her emoji and "lol" are friendly clues. If unsure, you can ask.
She wants you to leave the group
Nothing in her message asks you to leave. The clues are playful.

situations.s: In four square, a kid named Yusuf says your ball was out. You think it was in.
situations.q: What is a fair way to handle it?
o: Suggest a do-over
Yes! A do-over is a fair and quick way to settle a close call. The game keeps going.
Argue until everyone agrees with you
Long arguments can stop the game. A do-over is faster and fair.
Take the ball and leave
Leaving ends the fun for everyone, including you.

situations.s: Your group is picking a recess game. Most kids want soccer. You wanted kickball.
o: Play soccer today and ask for kickball tomorrow
Yes! Being flexible keeps friendships strong. Taking turns with games is fair.
Refuse to play at all
You might miss out on fun. Your game can have a turn another day.
Tell everyone soccer is boring
That can hurt feelings. Suggest your game for next time instead.

situations.s: You came in second in the class spelling bee. Kenji won.
situations.q: What is a good-sport thing to do?
o: Say "Nice job, Kenji" and feel proud you tried
Yes! Being a good sport shows respect. Second place is a big deal too!
Say the words were unfair
Blaming the words can make others feel bad. You did great work.
Refuse to talk to Kenji
Kenji did not do anything wrong. Being kind keeps your friendship.

situations.s: You are playing a video game with your cousin Isabela. She is losing a lot and looks frustrated.
o: Offer tips, or suggest a game you both enjoy
Yes! Helping or switching shows you care about her fun too.
Keep winning and cheer loudly each time
Loud cheering when someone is losing can feel like teasing.
Tell her she is bad at games
That can hurt. Everyone is learning.

situations.s: You are captain picking teams. Your best friend is not the fastest runner.
situations.q: What is a fair way to pick?
o: Pick your friend, and mix faster and slower runners so teams are even
Yes! Even teams make games fair and fun for everyone. Friends feel included.
Only pick the fastest kids
Uneven teams can feel unfair. The other team might not have fun.
Pick your friend last to win
That could hurt your friend. Fun matters more than winning.

situations.s: While playing cards, you notice Fatima peeking at other players' cards.
o: Say kindly, "Let's all keep our cards hidden so it's fair"
Yes! A calm reminder about the rule helps everyone play fair.
Yell "CHEATER!" in front of everyone
Yelling can embarrass her and start a fight. A calm reminder works better.
Peek at cards too
Two wrongs do not make it fair. The game works best when everyone follows rules.

situations.s: You and Arjun both want the last swing. You got there at the same time.
o: Take turns: count to 50, then switch
Yes! Counting turns is fair and quick. You both get to swing.
Push ahead and grab it first
Pushing is not safe and not fair.
Tell a teacher Arjun is being mean
Arjun did not do anything mean. You can solve this together.

situations.s: The substitute gives directions quickly. You did not understand the second step.
o: Raise your hand and ask, "Could you repeat step two?"
Yes! Asking is a smart skill. Other kids may have the same question.
Guess and hope it is right
Guessing can mean redoing work later. Asking saves time.
Do nothing until the end of class
Waiting means you miss the chance to learn. Ask now.

situations.s: Someone in your group chat keeps sending mean messages about your friend.
situations.q: What is a helpful thing to do?
o: Show a trusted grown-up and don't join in
Yes! Grown-ups can help stop online meanness. Not joining in shows you stand with your friend.
Send mean messages back
That can make things worse. A grown-up can help.
Ignore it and say nothing ever
Your friend might need help. Telling a grown-up is being a good friend.

situations.s: In your group project, you have too much work and your partners have very little.
o: Say, "Can we split up the tasks so it's even?"
Yes! Sharing work fairly is part of teamwork. Speaking up helps everyone.
Do all the work and feel upset inside
Keeping it inside can make you stressed. It's okay to ask for a fair split.
Quit the group
Quitting leaves the project unfinished. Talking about it helps more.

situations.s: You finished your part of the group project. Your partner Benjamín looks stuck on his part.
o: Ask, "Do you want help, or would you rather try on your own?"
Yes! Offering help and letting him choose is kind. Some people like to figure things out.
Take his part and do it for him
Taking over can make him feel left out. Ask first.
Say, "Hurry up, you're so slow"
Rushing him can make him feel worse. Everyone works at their own speed.

situations.s: You have a big science project due in two weeks. You do not know where to start.
situations.q: What is a good first step?
